surprise: check_ledger validates a ledger entry's 'rediscovered' field against clause ids scraped by the pattern '(clause: X)', but that pattern appeared ZERO times across all twenty node files — only '(kill_test: X)' was used, 39 times. clause_ids was therefore always the empty set and every value of --rediscovered failed, verified against four spellings. The rediscovery rate is the build's only instrument for detecting packet-assembly failure, and it was unusable by construction.
resolution: Assigned an explicit stable id to all 52 clause lines across the 20 node files, as '(clause: <node>/c<n>)'. Tie-break rule 7 (explicit over inferred) chose a declared id over deriving one from the kill_test path, which is also unavailable on ADVISORY clauses. No clause's meaning, force, origin or kill test changed; the constitution was not touched and no line was added to any file.
clause: every clause line in every node file carries a unique (clause: id); a clause with no id cannot be named by a ledger entry, so its rediscovery is unrecordable and the packet-assembly signal loses it silently

surprise: The gate's own guards had never been watched fail. Operating-loop step 7 is applied to every node's demons but the gate enforcing those demons carried no negative check of its own.
resolution: Installed a defect against each guard in a throwaway copy of build/ and confirmed the gate goes red: constitution cap, regressed seam, demon marked killed with a pending negative check, BINDING clause stripped of its kill test, corrupt JSONL register line, and an absent build directory exiting non-zero. All six fire. Reverting the clause-id repair turns three tests red, which is that repair's negative check.
clause: the gate is negative-checked like any other guard; a guard nobody has watched fail is not known to work, and that applies to the mechanism enforcing the rule as much as to the nodes it enforces it on

surprise: The packet-assembly rule is the mechanism the whole build's O(node degree) claim rests on, and it was specified in README.md but had no implementation — it was enforced by agent discipline alone. The plan's own position is that discipline is what this structure exists to replace.
resolution: Wrote scripts/packet.py: assembles the packet per the README rule, emits neighbour contracts as assume+guarantee only with upstream and downstream labelled apart, runs the can-i-build gate before emitting, and refuses on a regressed inbound seam. Measured the claim across all 20 nodes: degree 15 -> 779 lines, degree 1 -> 306, largest packet 39.3% of the build. Adding a non-neighbour node leaves a packet byte-identical, which is the claim stated as a test rather than as prose.
clause: an agent never reads build/; it receives a packet from scripts/packet.py, and neighbour clauses, demons, oracles and metamorphic relations do not travel across a node boundary

surprise: The first no-bleed guard was vacuous against half its hazard. It matched section headings at '## name', but packet.py emits a neighbour's sections one level deeper at '#### name', so leaking neighbour DEMONS passed the guard silently. Clause bleed was caught only because clause ids are unique build-wide; demons, oracles and metamorphic relations carry no ids and had nothing standing between them and a packet.
resolution: Matched the heading at any depth, and ran the negative check for each of the four reasoning sections separately rather than for clauses alone. Leaking neighbour demons now goes red. This is n.assembly/c3 rediscovered from the outside: two guards for one hazard is how the hazard survives, each obeyed in its own layer, with the failure living in the gap between them.
clause: a no-bleed guard is negative-checked against every section it is supposed to stop, not against the one that happens to carry an id

surprise: Two count drifts in build/README.md, both load-bearing. It told Phase -1 to 'Run the fourteen' while the register held sixteen prefabs — and an agent that runs fourteen leaves two prefabs unprobed, which is precisely what blocks a node from being opened. It also split the sixteen as 'Six carry evidence / Ten have none', a two-way split that matches no reading of the register: there are five carrying parallel-build evidence, two carrying only Palantir documentation, and nine carrying none.
resolution: Corrected the probe count to sixteen and the constitution line count from 146 to 148. Replaced the two-way evidence split with the three-way one the register actually supports, naming palantir-mcp and foundry-cli-superrepo as documentation-derived — the weaker kind of evidence, and the reason they are still probes rather than settled. Then moved prose drift off the phase-boundary audit's duty list and into CI: tests/build/test_plan_prose.py re-derives every count the README states from the registers themselves, and fails loudly if the sentence carrying a claim is rewritten away rather than passing vacuously.
clause: every count build/README.md states about itself is re-derived from the registers in CI; a stale count in the plan's own account of itself misroutes the work order, and this one did

surprise: The @osdk/generator register entry named the wrong mechanism, and the reality is worse than the claim. The generator does NOT keep emitting an older version — it is faithful to its manifest, and moving a fixture function 1.1.0 to 1.2.0 moves the emitted literal. The actual decoupling is that the literal is DECORATIVE BY DEFAULT: fixedVersionQueryTypes defaults to empty, applyQuery then sends no version at all, and the server resolves the latest published version, which may be a pre-release, per call. A stale pin is at least deterministic and diffable; an unpinned call can change invoked version between two identical deployments with no artifact changing anywhere. Confirmed on the wire against a stub fetch, and the silence half holds — a server reporting 9.9.9-DISAGREES against a client literal of 1.2.0 produced no error and a successful call, because applyQuery never compares them.
resolution: Tightened n.surface/c1 rather than changing any guarantee: read isFixedVersion as well as version, and where isFixedVersion is false report the invoked version as unknown rather than reporting the literal. Anyone acting on the register's original mechanism would have hunted staleness in the generated client, which is correct. Opened G035 on n.det_core, because a function whose invoked version is chosen server-side per call collides with the guarantee that every computed result carries its algorithm version. The shipped pinning rule was established by execution: a function is pinned if and only if its import-list entry carries an explicit apiName:version suffix, and the external-packages branch returns an empty list unconditionally so those are always unpinned. Membership is an unvalidated Array.includes, so a namespace-qualified or misspelled entry silently unpins what it was meant to pin — which is why the pin needs an assertion rather than a convention.
clause: the invoked function version is read from isFixedVersion and version together, and reported as unknown when unpinned; a version literal displayed as provenance while the client sends none is a plausible value that means nothing

surprise: The @osdk/react register entry is confirmed but overstated, and the overstatement would have cost an architecture decision. 'renderToString throws for any data-bound screen' is false: under a Suspense boundary renderToString emits the fallback plus a switch-to-client marker and does not throw, renderToStaticMarkup renders the shell, and renderToPipeableStream keeps the shell. Separately, useOsdkAction never calls useSyncExternalStore at all, so an action-only screen server-renders fine — and that is exactly the shape of the 7 CFR 1b.11(a)(46) determination-recording screen.
resolution: SSR is not barred for n.surface. Only data content inside a boundary defers to the client, which is the ordinary streaming-SSR posture rather than a limitation to design around. The probe now pins the Suspense dimension, which the original had no assertion for — it passed only because it hard-coded the unwrapped case, the one shape a real streaming app never ships. Two traps carried forward: grepping for the identifier getServerSnapshot is the wrong test, since that string appears nowhere in the shipped build even at the one 3-argument call site, so count call-site arguments instead; and useOsdkObjects throws 'No OsdkProvider found' synchronously before ever reaching useSyncExternalStore, so a probe without a provider sees the wrong error and can conclude the limitation is absent.
clause: a server-render limitation is pinned at the dimension the application actually ships — inside a Suspense boundary — not at the unwrapped case that is cheapest to write a test for

surprise: The useOsdkFunction register entry named the wrong type, the wrong package and the wrong symptom, while its conclusion survived. NotOptionalParams is a module-local unexported type in @osdk/client, not something the hook wraps. The real defect is one level below in OptionalQueryParams, which despite its name collects the REQUIRED keys — the polarity is exactly inverted. And at this build's stated dimension the symptom is backwards: for a query whose only parameter is an optional nullable string, omitting it is the ONLY thing that compiles, with no cast, and supplying it fails. The claim is true one fixture over, in the mixed case, where a nullable parameter comes out required and a non-nullable one comes out optional.
resolution: Recorded the real locus so a later session does not go looking in @osdk/react's type algebra. The register's locus sentence survives — the mismatch is in the binding, not the function, since executeFunction accepts the same calls with no cast because it prefers the generator-emitted signature. Also recorded a methodological trap that nearly produced a false green: @osdk/client ships two declaration trees and nodenext picks by the consuming package.json type field, so a mutation test against one tree while tsc reads the other confirms whatever you already believed. Both trees agree here, but check the one the app loads.
clause: a type-level probe states which declaration tree it compiled against; mutation-testing a tree the application never loads confirms the belief rather than the binding

surprise: The @osdk/react-components register entry set the wrong disqualifier, so its own test would have passed and produced the wrong decision. It said the buy dies if ObjectTable cannot host a constrained select plus a free-text justification per row. ObjectTable can host all three, at our exact six-element shape. The real disqualifier is that objectType is a REQUIRED prop and the component fetches its own rows from a live ontology, so it cannot be handed six local rows at all. There is also an escape hatch nobody knew about: BaseTable, from the same subpath, is generic over any row type and compiles against our exact shape with no ontology — so buy-or-build was never binary.
resolution: G022's hand-built default stands, for different reasons than it assumed, and the gap now records those reasons. The partial buy still loses: the write-back is not included, the dropdown is bound to no Foundry value set so the value set is hand-maintained either way, and the price is about 194 KB gzipped for one six-row checklist. The revisit conditions are assertions inside the probe rather than a note in the gap — objectType becoming optional, the table learning to write back, or the dropdown becoming type-bound each turn a named assertion red.
clause: a buy-before-build probe states the disqualifier it is actually testing; a probe aimed at the wrong hinge passes and returns the wrong decision, which is worse than not running it

surprise: Three things about foundry-cli-superrepo that the register did not anticipate. (1) The foundry CLI is not on npm or PyPI in any form; it is served from each enrollment's own artifacts registry, so this probe cannot be delegated to an unenrolled machine or agent at all — a stronger constraint than 'may not be available on this enrollment', and one on WHO can run Phase −1. (2) The prefab is not wholly enrollment-gated: the complete Ontology-as-code to IR to full metadata to OSDK TypeScript chain runs offline, deterministically, with no token. (3) The register states on Palantir's roadmap authority that Python functions are NOT supported in SuperRepo and binds n.drafter on it, but the shipped client carries /local-python-functions as a first-class proxy route, a full PY_RUNTIME with specs and execute endpoints, and a changelog naming python-functions as a real service.
resolution: Recorded the Python-functions contradiction as unresolved rather than deciding it, per tie-break rule 3 — either the roadmap is stale or the client is built ahead of a server not yet enabled, and no offline evidence discriminates. It is step 5 of the enrollment runbook. The offline half reduced G031 to one unknown: the SuperRepo shape is now known — foundry.yml as root marker, .palantir/ discovery, four services, and the React client fixed at exactly src/client.ts. n.ontology is therefore no longer waiting on this prefab and can develop and regenerate object types now. Also recorded a live version seam in the G032 fallback: at current public latest-vs-latest, the OAC vite plugin reads irContent.blockData while maker emits ontology, and the plugin throws at stage two.
clause: a documentation-derived roadmap claim is not evidence about a shipped artifact; where the artifact and the roadmap disagree the disagreement is recorded as open, not resolved toward whichever source is more convenient

surprise: The PIC crosswalk carries a trap that would have put three wrong properties on every mapped object type. NINE columns appear on all thirteen entities, but only SIX of them are the provenance properties n.ontology guarantees to carry onto every mapped type — the other three are id, created_at and other. An implementation that derives the provenance set by asking which columns are universal would carry all nine.
resolution: Take the provenance set from the source's explicit enumeration, which the repo README states, rather than deriving it from universality — tie-break rule 7. The probe asserts the nine-member universal set alongside the six-member provenance set so the distinction stays visible rather than being rediscovered. G007 is confirmed: (entity, property) is unique across 292 records with no duplicates. The obligation n.ontology takes on is now a number — thirteen entities, each needing an object type or a recorded reason it has none, derivable only from the CSV and enumerated nowhere in the documentation.
clause: the provenance property set is taken from the source's own enumeration, never derived from which columns happen to be universal

surprise: Federal Register cannot be asked the one question n.authority_ledger exists to answer. Its structured CFR filter requires an integer part, so `conditions[cfr][part]=1b` is rejected outright with HTTP 400 and `part=1` silently answers about a different part — 76 documents titled 'Documents affecting 7 CFR 1'. The register recorded this prefab's open question as rate limit and page size (G006); the real constraint is that the authoritative filter does not accept the part, which is a different and worse problem than a slow one.
resolution: Recorded as G036 rather than worked around. The lineage must be assembled from full-text term search (902 hits for the quoted citation) and then cross-checked against eCFR's per-section source credits, because term search is a recall instrument and n.authority_ledger's guarantee is completeness — a lineage that silently omits an amendment is indistinguishable at the point of use from a complete one. Also noted: paging is cursor-based via search_after_cursor, so a paged retrieval is not resumable from a page number alone.
clause: the amendment lineage is verified against a second source before it is emitted, because the authoritative filter cannot name Part 1b and term search cannot prove completeness

surprise: G033 assumed the environment was at fault and it was — but the same closure exposed that the plan's own recorded blocker was never the binding one for the Foundry half. G034 named four things missing: enrollment, credentials, CLI, MCP server. Three were present or configured all along. The single actual cause was that Node was not installed on the machine at all, so `npx -y palantir-mcp` could never launch, and the absence surfaced as 'no MCP server connected' — a symptom recorded as if it were the cause.
resolution: Egress closed G033 on evidence: 7 CFR Part 1b retrieved whole, twelve sections, byte-identical across two processes. G034 narrowed to one item — a session restart — after installing Node v24.19.0 from a checksum-verified official tarball. The general lesson kept: a blocker written down as a compound of four unreachable things was never re-tested item by item, so the one that was actually load-bearing stayed hidden behind three that were not. Compound gaps get decomposed before they are believed.
clause: a gap naming several missing things is re-tested per item at review, never as a unit

surprise: A working MCP server is not evidence that the credential configured for it is valid. palantir-mcp@0.14.0 answered live ontology reads all session while the FOUNDRY_TOKEN in ~/.mcp.json was EXPIRED — /multipass/api/me returned Default:Unauthorized with parameters.error = EXPIRED for that exact token. The reason is that palantir-mcp on npm is a wrapper, not the server: it downloads @palantir/mcp from the enrollment's own artifacts registry at ri.artifacts.repository.discovered.foundry-mcp and holds a separate credential at ~/.palantir/mcp-config.json, mode 600. G034's recorded plan was that the MCP server exercises the token itself on connection and that this is the right place to learn its validity. That plan would have reported a valid token where there was none, because the server never exercises the configured token at all.
resolution: Two credentials on two paths, tested apart, never inferred from one another. Token validity is established only by an explicit call to /multipass/api/me — 200 for live, Default:Unauthorized with parameters.error = EXPIRED for dead — and never by observing that an MCP tool answered. scripts/foundry_api.sh now resolves a token from FOUNDRY_TOKEN, then ~/.palantir/sr-token, then ~/.mcp.json, makes the call and never prints the credential, so the check is one command instead of an ad-hoc pipeline the permission classifier refuses. Recorded in CLAUDE.md so a new session reads it before debugging an auth failure rather than after.
clause: credential validity is asserted by an identity call that returns 200, never inferred from an unrelated client that happens to be working; two credentials on two paths are two facts

surprise: A 200 is not evidence until a bogus sibling returns something else. The first SuperRepo availability reading was /workspace/code/superrepo returning 200, which looked like the in-platform install flow being served. It is an SPA shell: /workspace/code/totally-bogus-xyz and /workspace/bogus-app-xyz return 200 with a byte-identical body, sha 7c6fb5ad59e2, 819 bytes each. That reading was discarded. What survived is the API layer, where /code/api/extension/install-script returns 200 and 4003 bytes against a 404 on /code/api/extension/does-not-exist — and the installer's named repository ri.foundry.cli.artifacts.repository then serves cli-linux-amd64-latest as 179411392 bytes of ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64. G032 is answered: SuperRepo IS available on this enrollment, against documentation that says it may not be.
resolution: Every availability claim carries its control in the same probe. A status code is reported only alongside what a deliberately invalid sibling of the same shape returned, and a downloaded artifact is identified by type and size rather than by the fact that the download succeeded — an HTML error page is also a successful download, which is why the shipped installer itself checks whether the first byte is '<'. G032 moves to ANSWERED and the MCP fallback is retained rather than deleted, because the namespace rule differs across the two paths: SuperRepo namespaces types at emission and the fallback must prefix them instead. The binary has not been executed and the enrollment half of the runbook has not run, so foundry-cli-superrepo stays probed:false and the gate still reports 11.
clause: an availability probe reports its control alongside its result; a 200 from a catch-all route and a 200 from a real endpoint are the same number and different facts

surprise: The build was one node away from creating object types that collide with a live prior build of the same system, in the same shared ontology, under names nobody had checked. Foundry holds a Phase 1A/1B tracer of SignatureReady built in Palantir's AI FDE: 6 object types under display prefix [SignatureReady] and apiName prefix Sr — SrProject, SrEnvironmentalDocument, SrCategoricalExclusion, SrTreatmentUnit, SrProposedAction, SrExtraordinaryCircumstanceScreen — plus 6 relations, an action type, sources S1 to S9, three repositories and a deployed app. build/ contains no Foundry RID and never mentions any of it, so n.ontology as written would have emitted duplicates into an ontology already holding ~1,225 types by many authors. The two builds also carry two gap vocabularies, GAP-A-## and G0##, tracking overlapping unknowns under different names.
resolution: The prior build is superseded, not extended — the operator's decision, recorded as a BINDING constitution section rather than a convention, because a naming convention with no assertion behind it is the same thing as no convention. Every resource this build creates is namespaced sr2: apiNamespace sr2 in foundry.yml where SuperRepo can enforce it at emission, and display prefix [SR2] with apiName prefix Sr2 on the MCP fallback path, which creates into the shared ontology where no namespace exists to carry. Nothing from the prior build is read as an input, imported or modified, and none of its identifiers are inherited — including its own claim that a later phase supersedes its tracer types, which is a claim about that build. Non-ontology resources are contained under PERSONAL PROJECT: christianpinkerton2; the object type is the one resource a folder cannot contain, which is what the prefix is for.
clause: an object type is created into the shared ontology and not into a folder, so containment for it is a name assertion rather than a location; every emitted type name is disjoint from the prior build's and carries the namespace prefix

surprise:
G001 is not 'unverified pending effort'. It is not answerable from ecfr.gov at all, because the thing it asserts uniqueness OF does not exist in the source. The versioner v1 API is structured at SECTION granularity only: is machine-readable, but

carries no attributes anywhere in Part 1b, so every paragraph designator is inline text and n.rule_corpus's (authority_id, citation) key must be derived. All three available derivations fail against the real bytes. Type-first depth collides 84 times, because c, d, i, l, m, v and x are simultaneously lowercase paragraph letters and roman numerals — live in Part 1b, not hypothetical: 1b.2(c) and 1b.2(d) are top-level letters that a roman-first reader nests under 1b.2(b)(2). Leading-tokens-only strands 30 designators, because a parent's opener can sit inline in a previous

— 1b.5(b) reads '(b) Scope of analysis. (1) In preparing' as one element — and the miss then cascades down the whole level. Consuming inline designators is unsound because 188 prose cross-references are shaped identically, e.g. 1b.7's 'See paragraph (e) of this section'. This also corrects PHASE-MINUS-1.md, which recorded G004 as answered 'at paragraph granularity'.
resolution: G001 stays open, with its reason changed from 'assumed unique' to 'not answerable from this source', which is a different instruction to whoever builds n.rule_corpus: do not write the parser and check uniqueness afterwards, because no parser available from this XML is both complete and unambiguous. The node needs either a second source of paragraph structure or an explicit derivation carried and tested as part of the node, whose uniqueness is then a property of that named derivation and of nothing else. The probe measures all three legs so the conclusion rests on counts. Two adjacent hazards are pinned in the same file: a 4-char-capped citation regex silently drops 15 of 1b.4's deepest entries, (xviii) through (xxxix), and 1b.4 IS the categorical-exclusion catalogue n.ce_catalog reads, so the demon truncates the CE list with no error anywhere; and a date past the title's most recent issue is a hard 404 naming that date, never a silent fallback, so a retrieval pinned to today fails loudly.
clause: citation uniqueness is a property of a named derivation, never of the document; a source that does not carry the key cannot be asked whether the key is unique

surprise: The Federal Register API silently wraps. Paging is offset-based — ?page=N works and pages 1 and 2 are disjoint, so the register's note that paging is cursor-based and not resumable from a page number is wrong — but the truth is worse than either reading. The page parameter is IGNORED past a ceiling of 50 and the response returns page one. At 20 per page over 902 hits for '7 CFR Part 1b': page 46 returns the last 2 rows, pages 47 to 50 return 0, and page 51 returns PAGE ONE'S ROWS at HTTP 200. A loop that walks a fixed number of pages re-ingests the head of the corpus as though it were the tail, with no error and no empty page to stop on, and n.authority_ledger's (authority_id, effective_date) key double-counts. per_page degrades the same way: 1000 and 2000 are honoured, 5000 returns 20 — the default — also at HTTP 200. No rate-limit headers exist at all. Separately, G036 is worse than recorded: conditions[cfr][part]=1b is HTTP 400, AND the rule's own cfr_references records part '1', so the API cannot represent Part 1b in queries or in metadata.
resolution: A paged retrieval terminates on a computed last page derived from the reported count, and asserts that the page past it is empty — never on 'keep going until a page looks wrong', because the wrapped page looks perfectly right. Any fixed-N page loop is a defect by construction. Page size is asserted against what was requested rather than assumed, since exceeding the ceiling is silent. Pacing is policy rather than feedback, because there is no header to back off on, which is the answerable half of G006. Tie-break rule 1 also forced a correction in the constitution, recorded here because it is the same probe: the source contract named '91 FR 17092 (2026-04-03)' as the authority version, but the rule published that day is document 2026-06537 cited 91 FR 17062, spanning pages 17062 to 17122. An FR citation names the START page, so 17092 is an interior page of that rule and the citation was wrong. Corrected in build/constitution.md. Its second citation, 91 FR 40353, is document 2026-13372 and was right.
clause: a paged retrieval stops at a computed last page and asserts the page beyond it is empty; a page index past the API's ceiling returns valid-looking rows from the head of the result set

surprise: Reachability was mistaken for retrievability. G033's closure note recorded that PNNL/NEPATEC2.0's 'tree and parquet readable anonymously despite gated auto'. Both halves are wrong: there are ZERO parquet files — the corpus is 505 JSONL — and no file content is anonymously readable. gated 'auto' blocks every file in the repository including .gitattributes, and datasets-server answers 401 for splits, first-rows and size. Only README.md and the metadata and tree APIs are public. So G011, row grain, is not work owed — it is a NEW BLOCKER on an authenticated HuggingFace identity that has accepted the gate, and with it go page-level text and the substring property n.precedent/c1 depends on. What the tree DOES give up is G012, because the corpus is partitioned by path as doc_type/agency: 60 of 505 files are USDA, 11.9%, non-trivial as assumed. Two findings make that number less useful than it looks. There is NO USFS bucket — the corpus carries exactly BLM, DOE, EPA, USDA — so n.precedent's 'USDA/USFS' filter is coarser than its contract implies. And the USDA slice holds 30 CE, 30 EA and ZERO EIS, against EPA's 230, so precedent coverage for the EIS and ROD paths cannot come from this corpus's USDA slice.
resolution: G012 is answered at FILE granularity and explicitly not at row granularity, and the probe says which so the number is not later quoted as a row count. G011 is reclassified from unmeasured to blocked, naming what unblocks it — a HuggingFace token whose identity has accepted the gate — so it is not repeatedly re-attempted anonymously. n.precedent's contract wording is now known to overstate its filter: USFS is not separable from USDA at any granularity visible without the data, so the ADVISORY clause about reporting selectivity must report what was actually filtered on. The zero-EIS finding is carried against the constitution's non-vacuity clause, which requires at least one emitted document of all five types: the EIS and ROD paths need a precedent source this corpus's USDA slice cannot supply. The probe asserts the 401s rather than tolerating them, so if the gate lifts it goes red and the news arrives.
clause: a source is retrievable only when its CONTENT has been retrieved; a tree listing, a metadata document and a 200 on a README are reachability and prove nothing about the rows
